items.title: Half a Billion Christians Around the World Can’t Access the Bible, New Analysis Shows
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: Concerning.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

While technology has greatly expanded the availability of Scripture, a perfect storm of calamities has kept the Bible out of the hands of half a billion Christians around the globe.

According to just-released data from the 2026 Bible Access List, the second such analysis from the Bible Access Initiative, 125 million believers are unable to access God’s Word in any format, even in countries where Scripture is technically allowed and safe to possess.

The report evaluates 106 countries and pinpoints where Christians face the greatest obstacles to accessing the Bible, some entirely and others in part.

“We often hear that the Bible is more accessible than ever, but we must not confuse availability with access,” Wybo Nicolai, co-founder of the Bible Access List, said in a statement about the latest data. “Persecution-related Bible access restrictions can make accessing Scripture difficult or dangerous, while socioeconomic barriers can put a Bible beyond people’s reach. Even where Scripture is available digitally, limited internet coverage or unsafe online environments can still prevent people from accessing it.”

Key barriers to access include persecution-related restrictions, social hostility toward Christians, threats from extremist groups, failing infrastructure, and socioeconomic issues, like poverty, lack of access to the internet, limited electricity, and illiteracy.

The top five countries on the coalition’s restrictions list (in order) are: Afghanistan, Yemen, Somalia, North Korea, and Eritrea.

“In Afghanistan, God’s Word is the most dangerous book any Afghan can possess,” the researchers stated. “And discovery can cost them their life. In North Korea, every dimension of Bible access is prohibited. Christians are treated as enemies of the state, and a Bible discovered in a routine house search can mean execution or a life sentence in a forced labor camp.”

The analysis looked at places, too, where believers don’t face legal restrictions but are suffering shortage of Bible access. Those top five countries (in order) are: the Democratic Republic of Congo (>10 million), Ethiopia (>10 million), Nigeria (>10 million), India (>10 million), and Uganda (5-10 million).

For context, there are more than 107 million Christians living in the DR Congo, but not even half — fewer than 33% — of believers there own a Bible in a country where it is legal to possess one.

“No law restricts access,” according to the report. “[But] the DRC is among the poorest countries in the world. Only about one in five people have electricity, and poor roads make remote communities difficult to reach in a country the size of Western Europe.”

items.title: Filmmaker Reveals What Charlie Kirk Said About Biblical Prophecy Before His Death
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "God's speaking to you."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Filmmaker Matthew Thayer’s new movie, “Can You Hear Me Now?” tackles biblical prophecy, exploring whether prophets still deliver messages to the masses today.

As part of the film, Thayer did one of the final interviews with conservative commentator Charlie Kirk before his assassination.

“I interviewed him with the impetus of talking to him about … the separation of church and state, Christian nationalism, all of the stuff that he was so eloquent at communicating,” Thayer said. “And it was a great interview.”

The filmmaker said he asked Kirk about prophecy and for his general take on whether it still occurs today.

“What he said blew me away,” said Thayer. “[Kirk’s] like, ‘Yeah, absolutely. I believe that there’s prophets, there’s prophecy — it’s a gift.’ It can be abused, but he’s seen it work and he’s seen it transform lives. But one of the things that he said that I thought was just right on was that a word from a prophet is not an excuse for … [inaction] or apathy.”

Kirk worried people might not have worked as hard as they could have in the 2020 election because they were relying on what they were told by a prophet and assumed it would be easily won.

“That actually, to me, points to a real fatalistic viewpoint that’s prevalent within the church of the will of God,” Thayer said. “That, if God speaks, it’s just going to happen. I don’t have to do anything about it. I can just pop some corn and sit on my couch and watch it all happen.”

Conversely, he said, a prophet’s role is to show up and alert people that situations are going the wrong way.

“A prophet’s word should be directional and actually require action upon the people and upon the people that are hearing it,” Thayer continued.

Ultimately, Thayer said he hopes “Can You Hear Me Now?” will inspire people to think deeper about how God might be speaking to them today.

“The biggest thing that was really kind of stuck with me the entire last year as we were making this film was all of the people that came out after Charlie Kirk’s death and were posting online going, ‘I’m being drawn to the Bible … Why do I want to go to church? I’m going to go to church’ — that was God speaking to all of those people.”

Thayer continued, “And so I really had a heart to really reach those people who are really infants in Christ and … kind of grab them by the collar and just go, ‘God’s speaking to you’ … because … there’s a whole swath of Christianity that doesn’t believe that God really kind of speaks.”

items.title: ‘We’re All Here Because of God’: Dak Prescott Says the Cowboys’ Open Faith Starts With Their Head Coach
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Dak Prescott says the Dallas Cowboys have gotten more open about their faith this season, and it’s no accident. After Sunday’s comeback win over the Houston Texans, the quarterback agreed with that observation in his postgame press conference. He credited head coach Brian Schottenheimer.
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Dak Prescott says the Dallas Cowboys have gotten more open about their faith this season, and it’s no accident.

After Sunday’s comeback win over the Houston Texans, the quarterback agreed with that observation in his postgame press conference. He credited head coach Brian Schottenheimer.

“Credit ‘Schotty’ and his leadership and the way that he’s opened that up,” Prescott said. “That’s who he is. That’s who I am. That’s who a lot of the guys on our team are.”

He said the goal is for it to spread. “Trying to be contagious and understand we’re all here because of God and we’re all here to serve a greater purpose.”

Prescott said the chaplains are part of it. “We’ve got great chaplains in Jonathan and Dr. Evans, and so they’re helping lead that cause.”

He said the same approach applies to how the team responds to results. “We may not always have the answers for it, but we know what God wants us to do in our response, and that’s be the best versions of ourselves, serving Him, serving others and doing it with just pure love.”

The Cowboys beat the Texans 34-30 in Houston to improve to 2-2. They trailed 16-6 at halftime and were behind 30-27 in the fourth quarter before Prescott led a 74-yard drive in 11 plays. It ended with a touchdown pass to CeeDee Lamb with 2:15 left. KaVontae Turpin’s 48-yard kickoff return to open the second half had set up the first touchdown of the comeback.

Prescott finished 32 of 45 for 335 yards and a touchdown. Lamb caught 17 passes for 189 yards and passed Drew Pearson for fourth on the Cowboys’ all-time receiving yards list, with 7,914 career yards.

After a loss the week before, Schottenheimer’s stated goal was “find a way to finish.”

He pointed to the locker room afterward. “These guys are a special group of young men that truly do love each other,” he said. “The brotherhood is real.” He called Prescott “flawless in the second half.”

Prescott said what he’s seen on the team starting with his coach is “special.”

“I’ve been through so much in my life,” he said. “God’s always been the reason and, yeah, who I fall back on and my refuge. I can’t thank Him enough and never will be able to thank Him enough.”

Win, lose or draw, he said, the question is the same: what’s the purpose?

items.title: Love in the Time of Acedia
items.author: Daniel Fitzpatrick
items.summary:
Daniel Fitzpatrick

The distractions of acedia—the temptations to turn aside from the order of the day—find an analog and inspiration in the rejection of worship.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Daniel Fitzpatrick

Sometimes an ordinary Wednesday can feel unbearable. The sun seems to hang forever on high. The iPhone screen repeats its sweet, incessant call. The work in front of me is never as compelling as the distractions I cultivate or the programs of action I imagine. The stack of ungraded essays leers at me until I rise, wraithlike, and glide once more into the faculty lounge for another cup of coffee, another quarter-hour’s conversation with a colleague beleaguered alike by sloth, the dismal demon that bids me look at everything the sun presents to me as part of God’s providence and say, with a sigh, “I’d rather not.”

I mention Wednesday not because sloth gains any greater potency in the midst of the journey of the week but rather for the example of Walker Percy, who liked to ask why it is that we often feel better in the middle of a disaster than we do in the day-to-day round of life. The sentiment is not without its privileged air. My own experience of Percy’s hurricane spirituality is that I do tend to feel a lot better when the power’s out and the wind is rattling the panes than when the sun is shining on my ordinary to-do list, that indeed the year after Hurricane Katrina—which flooded the home I grew up in and sent my family and me on a whirlwind survival tour of the South—was among the most enjoyable of my life. But that enjoyment was in part, at least, the privilege of a fourteen-year-old whose father exercised an impressive capacity for turning disaster into adventure. Nonetheless, I persist in holding with Percy that the temptation to give in to something very nearly like despair in the face of the ordinary good things of life, a tendency he captures in characters like Binx Bolling and Dr. Tom More, is among the more insidious snares laid by the enemy of human nature.

Less glamorous than pride, not so sexy as lust, nestled deeper in the bloodstream than wrath, sloth—also known as acedia—has garnered significant attention in literary and theological circles in recent years. Bishop Barron mentions now and then in his sermons that Karl Barth called acedia the besetting sin of the modern age. Evelyn Waugh called it the same in a review of a book of short stories by J. F. Power, and sloth figures prominently in the spiritual struggles of Waugh’s characters, perhaps most of all in Guy Crouchback, protagonist of the The Sword of Honor trilogy. More recently, R. J. Snell’s book Acedia and its Discontents has shed fresh light on the sway of sloth over the contemporary soul. All the same, sloth seems on the surface ill-suited to a place at the forefront of sin’s sallies against us. In the age of the grind, the hustle, the side-gig, the influencers, the macro-trackers, and the optimizers, we surely couldn’t be beholden to so slow and languid a sin as sloth. Sloth is an algae-ridden jungle freak with a dopey grin. Sloth is a lazy Sunday on the crumb-ridden couch. Sloth is an hour’s dilly-dallying before I do my homework. How could sloth be the besetting sin of the modern age?

But sloth, St. Thomas says, is not simply laziness. It is no mere spiritual lassitude such as might possess anyone after a long morning’s work and a heavy lunch. Rather, sloth is, in its deadliest form, “sorrow for spiritual good.” Sloth is sorrow occasioned by God’s will. It is, in its final moment, sorrow for heaven itself. 

The history of acedia is a long and storied one, with roots stretching into Homer, whose Achilles, withdrawing from battle and singing anguished songs on the beach, has drifted into a grand indifference. Michael C. Jordan notes that Nestor says of Achilles that the latter has no care (ou kēdetai), relating Achilles precisely to the Greek term (a-kēdos, un-caring) from which we derive the term acedia. Perhaps the richest accounts of acedia, however, come from authors such as Evagrius Ponticus and John Cassian, who refer to acedia as the noonday devil of Psalm 91 and describe in stirring detail its effects on desert monks. Such monks, laboring from an early hour in the desert heat, were often afflicted around noon with a deep listlessness, a grand distaste for returning to prayers or work. The temptation in such moments was to wander about, seeking idle conversation, or to stand outside and watch in desperation as the sun so slowly wandered westward. Likewise, such a monk might begin to dream up far off monasteries, where better architecture, better preaching, better food, and the like would allow him at last to achieve holiness. He might take on extra tasks, even charitable ones, to distract himself from his proper duties.

I confess that whenever I read these accounts, my scalp begins to prickle. A desire to get up and head once more to the faculty lounge washes over me, and it’s only a strong decoction of Aquinas and Percy that keeps me from it. How easy it is to distract myself from the work at hand, to scroll away a few seconds, several minutes, an hour. How little I want to do the plain tasks suggested by providence.

The distractions of acedia—the temptations to turn aside from the order of the day—find an analog and inspiration in the rejection of worship. To worship is at once to find authentic rest in God and simultaneously to perform our highest contemplative activity, to begin in temporal life the joyous action of eternity. And St. Thomas notes incisively that acedia “is opposed to the precept about hallowing the Sabbath day. For this precept, in so far as it is a moral precept, implicitly commands the mind to rest in God: and sorrow of the mind about the Divine good is contrary thereto.” That sorrow is perhaps most familiar to us in the form of the so-called “Sunday scaries,” that gentle despair that stirs itself of Sunday mornings and settles securely around the heart when the last NFL play of the day has been called and the spectre of Monday rises unimpeded from the impending night. Even as a child in a home of churchgoers, among folks who ate a big Sunday dinner together and played outside together and prayed the Rosary together at the end of the day, I felt those blues keenly. It was as though Sunday, rather than overflowing into the rest of my week, ordering my thoughts and actions, my labor and play, to the final work and play of the Father, was invaded by the cares of the workaday world. Nor was I alone in this, as meme after meme attests. (I am particularly fond of one in which the “Sunday scaries” take the form of an orangutan riding a tricycle in hot pursuit of a terrified child.) It occurs to me that, where Sunday is concerned, we have culturally become so many pharaohs to ourselves, hardening our hearts against the offer of communion with God, giving ourselves ever greater work quotas, denying ourselves the necessary straw. Meanwhile, the Lord beckons from the slopes of Sinai, bidding us be free—and free not simply from pharaoh but for him.

Order Your Set Today

Nor is the Lord content simply to call from afar. The king labors alongside his people in the vineyard, and Christ himself gives an example of how to reject acedia in his encounter with the Samaritan woman at the well. We recall that the account begins around noon, the moment when the desert monks so often felt acedia’s advance. Hungry, thirsty, weary with the journey and, we might imagine, with certainty of the disciples’ behaviors, Christ sits beside the well and waits as the woman approaches. (How often does that woman approach me in the form of one of my children asking for a cup of water or a wrestling match or another round of story time?) Here she stands—a sinner, an outcast, a burden. How easy to ignore her, to let her come and go and leave the silence undisturbed again. But Christ, the new Adam, engages her, prompts her, draws her out, and names her whole life for what it has been. The new Jacob, he rolls away the stone from her heart that this Rachel might draw water and be made whole. Like us in all but sin, Christ may have known the temptation to give in to sloth, to let the ordinary weariness of the day bleed into weariness over the other as an occasion to cooperate with providence. Rather, he pursues the goodness to be found in the fallen world, and in doing the will of the Father, he has food and drink.

St. Thomas says that sloth is overcome not by flight but by resistance. The trick, R. J. Snell says, looking again to the desert monks, is to stay in the cell, to say the prayers and do the work those in authority have set before me. To those of us not bound by monastic rule, the Samaritan woman—and Christ’s love for her—suggest several ways for overcoming sloth, beginning with reception of the sacraments. We come to Christ in the Eucharist, in the confessional, in the waters of Baptism, and there he shows us ourselves, soothes the thirst that’s sent us in search of him in all the wrong places.

The true Christian, as John Paul II reminds us in Dies Domini, is the one who is always living in Sunday, allowing its joys to overflow into every moment. Liturgically and sacramentally refreshed by Easter come round to greet us anew each week, we can reject acedia and share in the work of Christ, seeing our spouses, our children, our pastors and fellow parishioners, our work and our leisure, and the places we call home as part of God’s providence for us. Such seeing is a matter of charity, the virtue to which St. Thomas says sloth is especially opposed. Charity itself is in part a matter of attention, of fostering not only a workman’s sense of duty to the materials of life but an artist’s sense of wonder at them. Binx Bolling says in The Moviegoer, “I refuse to be distracted from wonder.” It’s easy to dismiss the notion as Binxian idealism, but for that matter, it’s easy to do the same with Christ’s injunction to be perfect. I take it that in heaven there will be no distracting the blessed from wonder and that many of the ones we call saints were well on their way to perfect attention by the hour of death. The invitation to wonder looks out from my children’s faces, flashes in the grass I trample on the way out each morning to work, awaits me in the words my students set to paper and in the difficult conversations the day might demand. To accept the wonder is to stand and fight.

Such seeing, of course, need not overlook mediocrity. Indeed, it bids us labor to make the conditions in which we live and worship and work as good as possible so as to glorify God. But it does demand that we reject the voice of acedia, the voice that says what God has given is not good. Christ waits for us, calls to us, bids us drink and be made wells of living water. If in the desert of sloth we feel the pang of thirst, we know at least that Christ, too, cried out his thirst from the cross, assenting to the Father’s will, pouring forth true drink for those who would rejoice in the moment of providence, seeing in it the way to the single moment of heaven.

items.title: Wednesday, October 7, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, our Gospel today gives us an opportunity to reflect on the Lord’s Prayer, the prayer for the Christian journey.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Galatians 2:1-2, 7-14

Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along with me. I went up in response to a revelation. Then I laid before them (though only in a private meeting with the acknowledged leaders) the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles, in order to make sure that I was not running, or had not run, in vain.

On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the gospel for the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been entrusted with the gospel for the circumcised (for he who worked through Peter making him an apostle to the circumcised also worked through me in sending me to the Gentiles), and when James and Cephas and John, who were acknowledged pillars, recognized the grace that had been given to me, they gave to Barnabas and me the right hand of fellowship, agreeing that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised. They asked only one thing, that we remember the poor, which was actually what I was eager to do.

But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood self-condemned; for until certain people came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles. But after they came, he drew back and kept himself separate for fear of the circumcision faction. And the other Jews joined him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy. But when I saw that they were not acting consistently with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas before them all, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?”

Psalm
Psalm 117:1bc, 2

Praise the Lord, all you nations!
    Extol him, all you peoples!
For great is his steadfast love toward us,
    and the faithfulness of the Lord endures forever.
Praise the Lord!

Gospel Reading
Luke 11:1-4

He was praying in a certain place, and after he had finished, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples.” He said to them, “When you pray, say:

Father, hallowed be your name.
    Your kingdom come.
     Give us each day our daily bread.
     And forgive us our sins,
        for we ourselves forgive everyone indebted to us.
    And do not bring us to the time of trial.”

Reflection

Friends, our Gospel today gives us an opportunity to reflect on the Lord’s Prayer, the prayer for the Christian journey. I want to consider three of the prayer’s petitions.

“Father, hallowed be your name.” We’re not implying that God should make his name holy (as though it isn’t); we’re praying that we might make it holy for us, that God might be honored above all. Everything else in the spiritual life flows from this prioritization.

“Your Kingdom come.” God’s kingdom refers to God’s way of ordering things. Jesus’s teaching and his manner of life give us a very good idea of what this kingdom would look like: peace, nonviolence, forgiveness, healing, walking the path of compassion. 

“Forgive us our sins for we ourselves forgive everyone in debt to us.” How central to the teaching of Jesus is forgiveness. And how central to the suffering of the world is the incapacity to forgive, both on the smallest, most intimate level and on the grandest geopolitical scale. 

How wonderful and how deeply challenging that at the very heart of the prayer that the Son of God taught us is a petition to be given the grace to forgive.
